Abstract
Enhancing the performance of drilling fluids by incorporating nanoparticles has significantly advanced drilling engineer­
ing, enabling the development of fluids with improved rheology, controlled fluid loss, and enhanced wellbore stability. 
Understanding the behavior of these advanced drilling fluids is essential for optimizing wellbore stability and minimizing 
formation damage. X-ray Computed Tomography (CT) is a high-resolution, non-destructive imaging technique widely 
used in petroleum and geoscience-related fields for quantitative analysis and 3D visualization. This study presents, for the 
first time, detailed Computed Tomography Number (CTN) measurements and 3D imaging of mud cakes and carbonate 
reservoir samples subjected to nanoparticle-based drilling fluids. The application of CT scanning provides crucial insights 
into mud cake structure and its role in stabilizing the wellbore. To investigate this, a novel dynamic high pressure high 
temperature (HPHT) filtration loop was designed to assess formation damage using drilling fluids enriched with green 
magnetite nanoparticles (NPs) and chitosan-coated green magnetite NPs. After circulating the drilling fluids through the 
loop, the produced mud cakes and core samples were analyzed using CT scanners. The captured X-ray images were 
processed with Hipax and Radiant Viewer to evaluate petrophysical properties such as porosity, permeability, density, 
and structural integrity. The results confirmed that high-performance water-based drilling fluids could mitigate formation 
damage in carbonate formations when formulated with an optimum concentration of 0.92% chitosan-coated magnetite 
NPs. The base drilling mud resulted in the highest formation damage, reducing porosity and permeability by 47.6% and 
85.63%, respectively, compared to only 3.33% and 9.8% reductions using the new nanoparticle-based drilling fluid sys­
tem. This study highlights the effectiveness of CT scanning for analyzing mud cake properties and assessing its role in 
protecting the formation from damage.

Introduction
Drilling fluid is a mixture of liquids, solids, and chemical 
additives that assists in the drilling of oil and gas wells. 
Initially, drilling fluids were primarily used for cuttings 
removal. However, with continuous advancements, they 
now serve multiple functions (Gautam et al. 2025). The 
term “mud” refers to a simple mixture of water and clay 
with some additives, whereas “drilling fluid” represents a 
more complex composition that includes chemical addi­
tives, materials, water, oil, and other components (Liu et al. 
2025; Cheraghian 2021).
Every year, millions of dollars are invested in improv­
ing drilling fluids to ensure successful drilling operations. 
Despite these advancements, challenges still arise due to 
unknown formation heterogeneity (Abdo and Haneef 2022), 
particularly in carbonate formations or when different rock 
types mix unexpectedly during drilling. The selection of an 
appropriate drilling fluid depends on the heterogeneity and 
composition of the formation (Zhang et al. 2021; Alfonzo 
et al. 2024). Additionally, the physical properties of the 
formation, such as temperature and pressure, influence the 
choice of additives, requiring specific formulations tailored 
to each formation (Valadbeygian et al. 2023). Drilling fluid 
plays a crucial role in enhancing drilling operations, making 
its functions essential for achieving efficiency and stability 
(Mahmoud et al. 2024).
Filtration is one of the important properties of drilling 
fluids that requires proper and sufficient attention. It is 
described as the loss of the liquid phase of the drilling mud 
into the encountered permeable formation due to the posi­
tive differential pressure (difference between the hydrostatic 
pressure and the pore pressure) (Lekomtsev et al. 2022). The 
liquid part of the drilling mud lost to the formation is called 
mud filtrate which is one of the main reasons behind the for­
mation damage (Rahmati et al. 2024). This issue causes the 
decline in oil and gas productivity in most reservoirs (Asad 
et al. 2024). Deposition of solid particles on the wall of the 
well forms the so-called mud cake (Gokapai et al. 2024). 
Fluid loss amount and the deposition of thin, impermeable 
and non-porous filter cake can mitigate the problems of 
sever formation damage (Carpenter 2019). Thus, the bet­
ter mud cake quality is required to prevent the drilling mud 
invasion into the formation (Rahmati et al. 2024).
Studies have declared that blending NPs into drilling 
mud, leads to improvement of the rheology and filtration 
properties which are playing a vital role in minimizing for­
mation damage, through controlling fluid loss (Ali et al. 
2020). Several researches have been published on nanopar­
ticle incorporation with the drilling mud to control formation 
damage by using a good and standard filtration quality. (Var­
gas et al., 2019) explored the effect of SiO2 NPs on the filtra­
tion quality of bentonite water-based mud. From their study 
they investigated that formation damage has been improved 
due to reducing the fluid lose by 67%. The effect of Fe2O3, 
Fe3O4, ZnO, and SiO2 nanoparticle in calcium bentonite 
drilling fluids on formation damage, filtration properties, 
and filter cake formation has been investigated at 300 psi 
and 250 oF by (Mahmoud and Nasr-el-din 2021). API filter 
press was used to evaluate and examine filtration property 
and formation damage through characterizing the deposited 
filter cake. API filter press involves calculating the rate and 
fluid amount that displaced from a porous medium (Khor­
mali et al. 2025). The results of that experiment declared 
that nanoparticle type affect the drilling fluid filtration prop­
erty, which in turn influences porosity percentage. Using 
0.5 wt% Fe2O3 NPs reduces the amount of damage in line 
with the average porosity by 1.0%. Comparatively, adding 
0.5 wt% of ZnO, SiO2, and Fe3O4 nanoparticle minimized 
the average porosity 30, 13.7, and 4.7% respectively. The

Filter press is a conventional method that is used to cal­
culate the volume of filtrate and thickness of filter cake of 
a mud sample. In addition to the filter press method, (Tan 
et al. 2021) have mentioned the role of laser apparatus and 
digital dial gauge method in measuring the degree of the 
filter cake thickness. According to the authors, laser method 
is a non-contact method of filter cake measurements; it has 
been used to deliver high precision cake thickness measure­
ment (Sazali et al., 2020).
Dial gauge method is another technique that is used to 
predict the thickness of the cake. It is an electronic measur­
ing device that measures the filter cake thickness at differ­
ent spots on the cake (Bageri et al., 2013). Dial gauge filter 
paper cake thickness measurement have lower or higher val­
ues than the laser measured cake thickness values (Elsayed 
et al. 2023). There are some uncommon methods that are 
mentioned in the literature but have not been used a lot such 
as a flat foot penetrometer and CAT scan and ultra-sonic 
(Amanullah and Tan 2000).
A number of researchers (Al-yaseri et al. 2015; Bageri 
et al. 2013; Bageri et al. 2021) have studied the morphol­
ogy, structure, and composition of the produced filter cake 
by using various advanced tools among them SEM, EDS, 
XRF and XRD analysis. Computed tomography (CT) scan 
approach was also used to detect the texture of the exter­
nal and internal layer of the filter cake. This approach is 
very useful for understanding reservoir formation damage, 
examining, visualization, quantify and qualify the reser­
voir heterogeneity. Throughout this technique uncertainties 
in core analysis can be minimized (Adebayo and Bageri, 
2020).
The major scope of this paper is documentation the 
impact of three different types of drilling mud; a conven­
tional bentonite water-based drilling fluid (base fluid), and 
two other drilling fluids one formulated by incorporating 
of uncoated green magnetite NPs and the other incorpo­
rated with chitosan coated green magnetite NPs on induced 
formation damage. A new dynamic filtration setup was 
designed, manufactured and installed to simulate the effect 
of three mud type’s circulation across carbonate core faces. 
Thus, the goal of this research is to: (1) investigate the influ­
ence of using uncoated and polymer coated green magnetite 
NPs on the filter cake characteristics of the carbonate core 
samples flooded by muds at HP/HT conditions (2) Explore 
the filter cake properties using a CT scan analysis. (3) Inves­
tigate the quality of the mud cakes and their damage degree. 
(4) Identifying the optimum content of the NPs that can 
incorporated to mitigate the formation damage.
Materials and methods
Materials
All the chemical reagents used (NaOH, ethanol, chitosan, 
Iron (III) chloride hexahydrate (FeCl3·6H2O) and iron (II) 
chloride Dihydrate (FeCl2·2H2O) are analytical grades pur­
chased from Merck and Aldrich chemical company. The 
base drilling fluid materials including bentonite, barite, and 
xanthan gum were purchased from Sigma Aldrich.
Preparation of the green uncoated and polymer-
coated MNPs
One-step biosynthesis process was performed to prepare the 
green Magnetite Fe3O4 NPs based on Cactus plant extract as 
the green source of the reducing agent. 25 g of the fresh Cac­
tus were refluxed in 250 ml distilled water for three hours at 
60 oC. Equal volumes of the Fe salts solutions were alkalin­
ized by 0.1 NaOH to pH 11 and stirred at 60 °C during the 
wisely dropping of the cooled and filtered plant extract. The 
pH of the reaction was kept at 11 during the reaction time of 
1 h. The NPs colloid was filtered, and the NPs were purified 
by washing three times with ethanol, then dried at 70 °C till 
constant weight. The dried NPs were characterized by using 
UV, XRD, EDX, and SEM (Faisal et al., 2023).
The coated green MNPs were prepared by coating the 
virgin MNPs with chitosan. The procedure was carried out 
by dissolving 0.1 g of chitosan in 15 ml acetic acid, then 
1.5 g of the magnetite NPs is added and the mixture was agi­
tated for 2 h at 60 °C. The cold solution was centrifuged to 
separate the coated magnetite NPs. The NPs were washed, 
dried and stored.
Formulation of the drilling fluids and carbonate core 
samples
The uncoated green MNPs and polymer coated green MNPs 
used in this study is based on the experiments performed 
by (Faisal et al. 2024). Bentonite, barite (BaSO₄), sodium 
hydroxide (NaOH), tape water, xanthan gum and green 
magnetic oxide nanoparticle are used in this study to pre­
pare smart drilling mud. Chemical reagents are purchased 
from the Merck and Aldrich chemical companies. Five dif­
ferent mud samples were prepared in the laboratory. The 
base fluid was prepared by mixing 15 g of bentonite, barite 
4 wt% and 400 ml of fresh water.

The manual saturator is used to inject water or brine into 
the sample. This device permits to perform a sequence of

standard apparatus includes a plug sized core cell, a vacuum

GasPerm
The GasPerm was used to measure the permeability of the 
core plug samples. The instrument can be used with any 
standard Hassler-type core holder. The device is connected 
to two Nitrogen supplies. One of 30 psig for the flowing 
gas and one of up to 400 psi for the confining pressure. The 
differential pressure transmitter was used to measure the dif­
ferential pressure at both ends of core sample.

a circulation system loop has been designed. To carry out 
the experimental work, a circulation system consists long 
pipe (1.5’’ OD) is designed. A core sample is placed into the 
designed core holder to study the interaction between the 
core and the drilling mud. The core holder has some impor­

It can be clearly pointed out that the water based-drilling 
mud shows an intensive formation damage for the carbon­

with the green MNPs. Using based-drilling mud, the poros­

Formation damage evaluation using X-ray 
computed tomography
Drilling fluids together with their solid particles can interact 
with reservoir rocks that cause a reduction in pore-perme­
able zones and prevent the hydrocarbon production, collec­
tively called formation damage. To evaluate the formation 
damage, the recent study used the drilling fluids with their 
different formulation and water-based drilling fluids in a 
dynamic condition through a new mud-circulation design 
to characterize the mud cake and reservoir core samples. 
This dynamic design is simulated to study the mud cake and 
core samples in conditions close to subsurface settings of 
reservoir carbonate core samples. The obtained mud cake 
and carbonate core samples in pre- and post-invasion were 
analyzed using X-ray computed tomography (CT) to draw 
a high-resolution model for formation damage. To obtain a 
high-resolution model in formation damage, a cross-section 
(CS) and longitudinal-section (LS) were considered in mea­
suring the CT number measurement (CTN).
This study uses for the first time both CS and LS analy­
ses for deep detailed and better understanding the formation 
damage in pre-invasion and post-invasion process. The LS 
analyses were used to observe the invasion direction of the 
drilling fluids along the core rocks, while CS were used to 
analyze and observe both mud cake and core sample altera­
tion along their diameters (Fig. 3). Because of the following 
reasons, the authors focus on the LS and CS analyses in mud 
cake and core samples to obtain the network observation 
and analyses: (i) The heterogeneity of the studied carbon­
ate core samples, (ii) non-homogenous (i.e., non-uniform) 
of mud cake thickness, (iii) to observe the involvement of 
drilling fluid along the whole cross sectional area, also the 
role of additives in drilling fluid in distribution and precipi­
tation of solid particles, will influence on the intensity of

Conclusions
This study demonstrates the effectiveness of green magne­
tite nanoparticles (MNPs) in optimizing drilling fluid per­
formance, mitigating formation damage, and enhancing 
wellbore stability through CT imaging analysis. The key 
findings are as follows:
	
●
Dynamic mud circulation was performed using drilling 
fluids with varying concentrations of green magnetite 
nanoparticles (MNPs), and the resulting mud cakes were 
analyzed.
	
●
CT imaging and CTN analysis provided insights into the 
structural properties, nanoparticle distribution, and po­
tential defects within the mud cake, optimizing drilling 
fluid formulations for enhanced wellbore stability.
	
●
Porosity and permeability measurements confirmed that 
drilling fluids with 0.92 wt% chitosan-coated MNPs re­
sulted in the lowest formation damage, reducing poros­
ity by 3.33% and permeability by 9.8%, while the base 
fluid caused significantly higher damage (47.6% poros­
ity and 85.63% permeability reduction).
	
●
Optimized MNP selection is crucial for producing high-
quality mud cakes that stabilize the wellbore, control 
filtration losses, and prevent fluid invasion into the 
formation.
	
●
Impermeable mud cake formation at the core inlet effec­
tively limits deep mud penetration, reducing formation 
damage and reinforcing the wellbore.
	
●
CT scan analysis validated the effectiveness of MNP-
enhanced drilling fluids in rapid mud cake formation, 
The CTN value of the mud cake layer deposited on the 
core surface incorporated with 0.92 wt% polymer coated 
green MNPs is depicted in Fig. 4E. The highest value of 
CTN with 1264 HU were recorded for polymer coated mud 
composition. Due to the uniform and highly compacted mud 
cake layer (CTN = 1264), the invasion of drilling mud into 
core rocks will decrease. Therefore, the CS and LS ranges 
in CTN for pre- and post-mud invasion were 32 and 37, 
respectively. This indicates that mud particle invasion for 
polymer coated mud composition is the lowest. Formation 
of a low-thickness mud cake on the wellbore wall with low 
porous and permeable zones are more noticeable for envi­
ronmental and industrial aspects (Khandaker et al. 2023). 
The produced thin mud cake layer reveals the precipita­
tion or exchanging of elemental/mineral composition dur­
ing fluid-solid interaction. To further approve the formation 
damage improvement for this mud type, the pre- and post-
porosity and permeability of the core sample was also mea­
sured. A reduction of 3.33 and 9.8% of core sample porosity 
permeability respectively were recorded. Thus, the CTN 
of the injected core sample with drilling mud of 0.92 wt% 
polymer coated with green MNPs in pre- and post-invasion 
were very similar and show a close compacted curves from 
inlet to outlet locations. This is a good indication that poly­
mer coated green MNPs drilling mud effectively blocks the 
pore spaces along the mud cake and the particle is fitted 
tightly into the available pore spaces, it is more difficult for 
the mud to sweep it away.
At higher temperatures, the nanoparticles is aggregated. 
However, polymer coated nanoparticle (PCNPs) stabilizes 
and hinders the nanoparticle agglomeration and settle­
ment. The recent study illustrates that the NPs filled the 
pore spaces in the structure of the mud cake and creates 
a uniform particle distribution, therefore reduces the fluid 
loss values to a minimum as compared to the base fluid 
(Fig. 4E). Recently, Polymer NPs have received important 
interest as additives to improve nanoparticle dispersibility, 
modify surface property and hence maintain their stability 
(Ali et al. 2020; Kareem and Kamal 2023). When nanopar­
ticles covalently attached to a very thin layers of polymers 
such as poly-acrylic acid (PAA), dextran, chitosan and oleic 
acid the stability of NPs could be preserved (Ju et al. 2020). 
The mud cake layer decreases the dynamic filtration rate 
and mud particle invasion, when compared to the base mud. 
This can be considered as a significant advantage for this 
mud sample that improves wellbore stability. Consequently, 
using 0.92 wt% polymer coated green MNPs to a base mud, 
the polymer adsorption results in low permeability and 
higher strength mud cakes which can resist the flow rate of 
mud circulation along the core face.

Abstract: Enhancing the performance of drilling fluids by incorporating nanoparticles has significantly advanced drilling engineer­ ing, enabling the development of fluids with improved rheology, controlled fluid loss, and enhanced wellbore stability. Understanding the behavior of these advanced drilling fluids is essential for optimizing wellbore stability and minimizing formation damage. X-ray Computed Tomography (CT) is a high-resolution, non-destructive imaging technique widely used in petroleum and geoscience-related fields for quantitative analysis and 3D visualization. This study presents, for the first time, detailed Computed Tomography Number (CTN) measurements and 3D imaging of mud cakes and carbonate reservoir samples subjected to nanoparticle-based drilling fluids. The application of CT scanning provides crucial insights into mud cake structure and its role in stabilizing the wellbore. To investigate this, a novel dynamic high pressure high temperature (HPHT) filtration loop was designed to assess formation damage using drilling fluids enriched with green magnetite nanoparticles (NPs) and chitosan-coated green magnetite NPs. After circulating the drilling fluids through the loop, the produced mud cakes and core samples were analyzed using CT scanners. The captured X-ray images were processed with Hipax and Radiant Viewer to evaluate petrophysical properties such as porosity, permeability, density, and structural integrity. The results confirmed that high-performance water-based drilling fluids could mitigate formation damage in carbonate formations when formulated with an optimum concentration of 0.92% chitosan-coated magnetite NPs. The base drilling mud resulted in the highest formation damage, reducing porosity and permeability by 47.6% and 85.63%, respectively, compared to only 3.33% and 9.8% reductions using the new nanoparticle-based drilling fluid sys­ tem. This study highlights the effectiveness of CT scanning for analyzing mud cake properties and assessing its role in protecting the formation from damage.
